# 0011: S3 key without a suffix, create-only write

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-19
- **Modules:** contract, upload-service, processor, local
- **Source:** design doc, section "How S3 keys stay unique" (linked from README.md in this folder)

## Decision

Keep the key with no suffix and write with `If-None-Match: *`, so S3 answers 412 instead of overwriting. The POC answers
429 on every collision; the retry-once-for-small-bodies refinement is not built. A collision needs the same phone,
type and millisecond, and nothing is lost on 429 (see ADR 0009).

## Rules for agents

Never write to S3 without `If-None-Match: *`, and never change the key format without a contract change and a new record.

1	# How uploads are laid out in S3
2	
3	All phones share one bucket. Each phone gets its own prefix inside it, named after its MAC. S3 has no real folders: a
4	`/` in a key is just a character, and the console and CLI use it to show prefixes as folders.
5	
6	The format is defined in code by
7	[`ObjectKey.java`](../../contract/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/contract/ObjectKey.java). If this page and the
8	code disagree, the code is right. The decision behind it is
9	[ADR 0011](decisions/0011-s3-key-with-create-only-write.md).
10	
11	## The bucket
12	
13	```
14	<device-logs-bucket>                 one bucket, shared by every phone
15	└── raw/
16	    ├── 0004f2abcdef/                phone 1 (a prefix, not a bucket)
17	    │   └── 2026-10-21/
18	    │       ├── 134512345Z-app.log
19	    │       ├── 134512901Z-boot.log
20	    │       └── 160230077Z-app.log
21	    └── 0004f2123456/                phone 2
22	        └── 2026-10-21/…
23	```
24	
25	`<device-logs-bucket>` is a placeholder; the real name is set per environment. A new phone needs no setup: its first
26	upload writes a key with a new MAC segment, and the prefix exists from then on.
27	
28	## One key
29	
30	```
31	raw/0004f2abcdef/2026-10-21/134512345Z-app.log
32	 │       │           │          │      └── file type: app.log, boot.log, calls.xml
33	 │       │           │          └── server UTC receive time, HHmmssSSS, then Z
34	 │       │           └── server UTC receive date
35	 │       └── MAC, 12 lowercase hex digits
36	 └── fixed prefix
37	```
38	
39	- The date and time come from the server's clock at receive time, not the phone's.
40	- The type is the base type. A manual `<mac>-now-app.log` upload gets the same kind of key as a normal one.
41	- There is no random suffix, so two uploads from one phone in the same millisecond would collide. The upload service
42	  writes with `If-None-Match: *`, so S3 answers 412 instead of overwriting.
43	
44	## One object
45	
46	One key maps to one body. The body is the file's bytes as the phone sent them. The upload service also attaches
47	metadata, and the processor reads it with one `HeadObject` call without opening the body. The field names are in
48	[`ObjectMetadataKeys.java`](../../contract/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/contract/ObjectMetadataKeys.java).
49	
50	| Field           | Meaning                                | Example (illustrative) |
51	|-----------------|----------------------------------------|------------------------|
52	| `user-agent`    | the phone's `User-Agent` header        | `<model>/<firmware>…`  |
53	| `source-ip`     | where the upload came from             | `203.0.113.7`          |
54	| `cert-serial`   | serial of the phone's mTLS certificate | `4F2A…`                |
55	| `manual`        | whether the phone sent a `-now-` file  | `false`                |
56	| `original-name` | the file name as uploaded              | `0004f2abcdef-app.log` |
57	
58	The example values are made up. The upload service decides what each field holds.
59	
60	## Looking at it
61	
62	```bash
63	# List every key in the bucket, with sizes in bytes.
64	aws s3 ls s3://<device-logs-bucket> --recursive
65	
66	# Show one object's metadata without downloading the body.
67	aws s3api head-object --bucket <device-logs-bucket> --key raw/0004f2abcdef/2026-10-21/134512345Z-app.log
68	```
69	
70	Add `--endpoint-url http://localhost:4566` to either command to run it against LocalStack.
71	
72	## Why one bucket
73	
74	- AWS limits the number of buckets per account, and bucket names must be globally unique. A bucket per phone would not
75	  scale and would add a create step to the first upload from every new phone.
76	- The upload service needs permission to write to one known bucket, not to create buckets
77	  ([ADR 0012](decisions/0012-eks-pod-identity-for-upload-service.md)).
78	- S3 sends one event per new object to SQS, so there is one notification setup and one queue
79	  ([ADR 0017](decisions/0017-s3-events-straight-to-sqs.md)).
80	- Putting the MAC first makes "all files for one phone" a single prefix listing.

# How uploads are laid out in S3

All phones share one bucket. Each phone gets its own prefix inside it, named after its MAC. S3 has no real folders: a
`/` in a key is just a character, and the console and CLI use it to show prefixes as folders.

The format is defined in code by
[`ObjectKey.java`](../../contract/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/contract/ObjectKey.java). If this page and the
code disagree, the code is right. The decision behind it is
[ADR 0011](decisions/0011-s3-key-with-create-only-write.md).

## The bucket

```
<device-logs-bucket>                 one bucket, shared by every phone
└── raw/
    ├── 0004f2abcdef/                phone 1 (a prefix, not a bucket)
    │   └── 2026-10-21/
    │       ├── 134512345Z-app.log
    │       ├── 134512901Z-boot.log
    │       └── 160230077Z-app.log
    └── 0004f2123456/                phone 2
        └── 2026-10-21/…
```

`<device-logs-bucket>` is a placeholder; the real name is set per environment. A new phone needs no setup: its first
upload writes a key with a new MAC segment, and the prefix exists from then on.

## One key

```
raw/0004f2abcdef/2026-10-21/134512345Z-app.log
 │       │           │          │      └── file type: app.log, boot.log, calls.xml
 │       │           │          └── server UTC receive time, HHmmssSSS, then Z
 │       │           └── server UTC receive date
 │       └── MAC, 12 lowercase hex digits
 └── fixed prefix
```

- The date and time come from the server's clock at receive time, not the phone's.
- The type is the base type. A manual `<mac>-now-app.log` upload gets the same kind of key as a normal one.
- There is no random suffix, so two uploads from one phone in the same millisecond would collide. The upload service
  writes with `If-None-Match: *`, so S3 answers 412 instead of overwriting.

## One object

One key maps to one body. The body is the file's bytes as the phone sent them. The upload service also attaches
metadata, and the processor reads it with one `HeadObject` call without opening the body. The field names are in
[`ObjectMetadataKeys.java`](../../contract/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/contract/ObjectMetadataKeys.java).

| Field           | Meaning                                | Example (illustrative) |
|-----------------|----------------------------------------|------------------------|
| `user-agent`    | the phone's `User-Agent` header        | `<model>/<firmware>…`  |
| `source-ip`     | where the upload came from             | `203.0.113.7`          |
| `cert-serial`   | serial of the phone's mTLS certificate | `4F2A…`                |
| `manual`        | whether the phone sent a `-now-` file  | `false`                |
| `original-name` | the file name as uploaded              | `0004f2abcdef-app.log` |

The example values are made up. The upload service decides what each field holds.

## Looking at it

```bash
# List every key in the bucket, with sizes in bytes.
aws s3 ls s3://<device-logs-bucket> --recursive

# Show one object's metadata without downloading the body.
aws s3api head-object --bucket <device-logs-bucket> --key raw/0004f2abcdef/2026-10-21/134512345Z-app.log
```

Add `--endpoint-url http://localhost:4566` to either command to run it against LocalStack.

## Why one bucket

- AWS limits the number of buckets per account, and bucket names must be globally unique. A bucket per phone would not
  scale and would add a create step to the first upload from every new phone.
- The upload service needs permission to write to one known bucket, not to create buckets
  ([ADR 0012](decisions/0012-eks-pod-identity-for-upload-service.md)).
- S3 sends one event per new object to SQS, so there is one notification setup and one queue
  ([ADR 0017](decisions/0017-s3-events-straight-to-sqs.md)).
- Putting the MAC first makes "all files for one phone" a single prefix listing.

1	# 0009: Specific status codes, require Content-Length, never 503
2	
3	- **Status:** Accepted
4	- **Date:** 2026-10-16
5	- **Modules:** upload-service, local
6	- **Source:** design doc, section "Status codes and Content-Length" (linked from README.md in this folder)
7	
8	## Decision
9	
10	Answer with specific codes and require Content-Length. Requiring a length lets the service stream with no buffering and
11	reject large files before reading them. Phones do not retry 429 and lose nothing: `app.log` carries its lines into the
12	next upload and the other files are full copies every time.
13	
14	The codes: 400 for a bad name or a body that ends before Content-Length, 403 for a disabled type or an identity
15	problem, 408 for a body that stops arriving, 411 with no length, 413 when too large, 429 for the rate limit, a key
16	collision and storage failures. Tomcat sends the 400 and 408 for a broken body itself; the service records the same code
17	so the log line matches what the phone got.
18	
19	## Rules for agents
20	
21	Never return 503, and never read the body before every check has passed.
22

# 0009: Specific status codes, require Content-Length, never 503

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-16
- **Modules:** upload-service, local
- **Source:** design doc, section "Status codes and Content-Length" (linked from README.md in this folder)

## Decision

Answer with specific codes and require Content-Length. Requiring a length lets the service stream with no buffering and
reject large files before reading them. Phones do not retry 429 and lose nothing: `app.log` carries its lines into the
next upload and the other files are full copies every time.

The codes: 400 for a bad name or a body that ends before Content-Length, 403 for a disabled type or an identity
problem, 408 for a body that stops arriving, 411 with no length, 413 when too large, 429 for the rate limit, a key
collision and storage failures. Tomcat sends the 400 and 408 for a broken body itself; the service records the same code
so the log line matches what the phone got.

## Rules for agents

Never return 503, and never read the body before every check has passed.

1	package com._8x8.herd.device_logs.upload.policy;
2	
3	/**
4	 * Why an upload is refused: one reason per check in {@link UploadPolicy}, then what can go wrong once the body is read,
5	 * in {@code upload.UploadFlow}. Each reason has its status code in {@code web.RejectionStatusMapper} and its response
6	 * in openapi.yaml, so adding one means updating both, and the parameterized web test.
7	 */
8	public enum Rejection {
9	
10	    /** The path after /logs/ is not an accepted file name. 400. */
11	    BAD_FILE_NAME,
12	
13	    /** The file type is turned off in device-logs.file-types, as calls.xml is by default. 403. */
14	    FILE_TYPE_DISABLED,
15	
16	    /** The ALB headers do not establish who is calling. 403. */
17	    UNTRUSTED_IDENTITY,
18	
19	    /** The certificate MAC differs from the MAC in the file name. 403. */
20	    MAC_MISMATCH,
21	
22	    /** The request has no Content-Length, for example because it is chunked. 411. */
23	    LENGTH_REQUIRED,
24	
25	    /** Content-Length is above the type's max-size. 413. */
26	    TOO_LARGE,
27	
28	    /**
29	     * The connection ended before Content-Length bytes arrived. Tomcat answers 400 itself when its read of the body
30	     * fails, so this records the same code.
31	     */
32	    BODY_INCOMPLETE,
33	
34	    /** The body stopped arriving for longer than Tomcat's connection timeout. Tomcat answers 408 itself, as above. */
35	    BODY_TIMEOUT,
36	
37	    /** An object already has this key, so the create-only write was refused and nothing was overwritten. 429. */
38	    KEY_EXISTS,
39	
40	    /** The write to storage failed or ran past its deadline. The file may still have been stored. 429, never 503. */
41	    STORAGE_FAILED
42	}

content.text:
I've read the S3 adapter, the upload flow, the client config and ADRs 0008, 0009 and 0011. Here's what happens.

**First, by default neither upload reaches S3.** `calls-xml.enabled` is `false` (ADR 0008), so both requests get **403** (`FILE_TYPE_DISABLED`) on headers alone. Everything below assumes calls.xml has been turned on in config.

**The S3 write:** The key is built from the MAC, the server's UTC receive time to the millisecond, and the file type. There is no random suffix, so both requests get the same key. Each is written with a single `PutObject` carrying `If-None-Match: *`. One wins. S3 refuses the other in one of two ways:
- **412** if the first object already exists.
- **409 `ConditionalRequestConflict`** if the first write is still in progress.

`S3LogStorage.isCollision` treats both as `StoreResult.KEY_EXISTS`, and nothing is overwritten.

**Status for the second request:** `UploadFlow` turns `KEY_EXISTS` into `Rejection.KEY_EXISTS`, which `RejectionStatusMapper` maps to **429**. It is never 503 (ADR 0009).

**Retry:** No. The S3 client uses `AwsRetryStrategy.doNotRetry()`. The body can only be read once, and a retry after a lost response would collide with the first write anyway. Phones don't retry on 429 either.

**Data loss:** No. The winning request stored the same bytes, and calls.xml is a full copy every time, so the next upload carries everything anyway (ADRs 0009 and 0011).

One edge case the repo doesn't cover, and this is my own inference: if the second request gets the 409 and the first write then fails, neither copy is stored. Even then, only that one upload is missed, because the phone's next upload is a full copy.

**Files used:**
- `upload-service/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/upload/storage/s3/S3LogStorage.java`
- `upload-service/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/upload/storage/s3/S3ClientConfig.java`
- `upload-service/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/upload/upload/UploadFlow.java`
- `upload-service/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/upload/policy/Rejection.java`
- `upload-service/src/main/java/com/_8x8/herd/device_logs/upload/web/RejectionStatusMapper.java`
